problems.description: Bare `except: pass` in `ensure_db` swallows all exceptions from `db.create_all()`, silently masking database failures and leaving the app in a broken state.
`db.create_all()` runs inside `before_request` on every request for file-backed DBs — needless overhead plus a race window for concurrent schema creation; should happen once at startup.
The `ensure_db` guard logic (`if not db.engine.url.database or ':memory:' not in ...`) is convoluted and inverts the apparent intent (runs create_all when a file DB exists, not when absent).
11 convention violations (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE naming across app.py, celery_config.py, models.py, repositories.py) hold the convention score at 0.69 — mostly trivial style, not structural.

Greenfield session discards the seed's Blueprint + raw-sqlite3 pattern wholesale (no Blueprints visible in the new app.py) in favor of SQLAlchemy models/repositories — expected for a rebuild, but the prior modular seams were already sound.

strengths: Modularized the monolithic app.py into a layered structure (models, repositories, Celery tasks, celery_config), which is the right architectural direction
SonarQube improvements confirm real quality gains: -3 smells, -4 cognitive complexity, +0 bugs and no added duplication
Added Celery configuration and background task layer — an idiomatic pattern for decoupling async work from request handling
commit_reviews.summary: A net improvement — meaningful modularization and lower complexity (SonarQube -3 smells, -4 cognitive complexity) — but the per-request `db.create_all()` with a bare `except: pass` and the low 0.69 convention score pull it short of clean.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as a placeholder ('your-secret-key-change-in-production') in app.py — it should come from an environment variable; a guessable, committed key makes the JWT auth trivial to forge and rotating it later invalidates every token.
token_required trusts user_id decoded from the JWT without verifying the user still exists in the DB, so tokens for deleted users continue to authorize access.
Auth logic (decorator + register/login routes) is inlined in app.py alongside routes; acceptable for the current single-file structure, but it will need extraction to a module as the app grows.

The 0.69 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py); the new code itself follows snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE norms.

strengths: Passwords are hashed via werkzeug.security (generate_password_hash/check_password_hash), not stored in plaintext.
Comprehensive test coverage added for the new endpoints (register success, duplicate username 409, missing username/password 400, login).
Ownership scoping applied consistently to all task routes with a 404 (not 403) on foreign tasks, avoiding information disclosure.
Auth implemented as a reusable token_required decorator rather than repeated inline checks.
Follows existing patterns: routes in app.py, existing db.session idioms, to_dict() extended, and the established test fixture structure.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent auth + per-user ownership feature that follows the existing Flask app patterns and ships with solid tests and proper password hashing, held back mainly by a hardcoded placeholder SECRET_KEY and a convention score inflated by pre-existing violations in files the commit never touched.

problems.description: Adding the User.email column with no DB migration — existing sqlite databases won't get the column unless recreated, so the notification feature silently no-ops on live data.

send_notification_email.delay() fires inside the request path after db.commit(); if the broker is unreachable the exception surfaces as a 500 on an already-committed transaction, with no after_commit wrapper or error handling.
test_notification_email_sent_on_completion and test_notification_email_sent_when_status_changes_to_completed are near-duplicates (differ only in the initial task status); low risk, but redundant.

strengths: Clean module separation — Celery app (tasks.py), config (celery_config.py) kept out of app.py, with proper queue routing and env-overridable broker settings.

Transition detection is correctly edge-triggered (only fires on the status → 'completed' edge, skipping already-completed and non-completion updates), and the email is sent after commit so the task is durable.
Comprehensive edge-case tests (no email on owner, other status changes, already completed) that mock app.send_notification_email and assert delay() call semantics.
Async dispatch (.delay()) means the response path isn't blocked on email I/O — the right shape for a notification integration.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested Celery notification integration that fits the session-3 story goal and existing app/test patterns; the only real blemishes are the un-migrated email column and unguarded .delay() in the request path.

problems.description: Dead code: `TaskRepository.update_task`, `TaskRepository.update_task_partial`, `TaskRepository.get_task_by_id_and_owner`, and `UserRepository.create_user` are defined with no callers in the diff; the overlapping `create`/`create_user`/`create_user_with_password`/`create_task` and `update`/`update_task`/`update_task_partial` families inflate cognitive complexity (+8 per SonarQube) for zero current benefit.

Incomplete refactor: the `update_task` route still mutates task attributes inline and calls `task_repo.save(task)` even though the repo already exposes `update_task_partial`; this leaves two coexisting persistence idioms (repo-encapsulated and route-inline), so the extraction is only partially applied.

Latent authorization smell: routes fetch tasks via unscoped `get_by_id` while the owner-scoped `get_task_by_id_and_owner` helper exists unused; the inline ownership check still prevents a real IDOR hole today, but the safer primitive is orphaned.

New module-level instances `user_repo`/`task_repo` in app.py are flagged as non-UPPER_CASE module constants, contributing to the 0.69 convention score; cosmetic but inconsistent with the flagged naming rule.

strengths: Introduces a clean, idiomatic repository abstraction (BaseRepository ABC) that decouples route handlers from direct SQLAlchemy model/query access, simplifying app.py (~-16 lines) and centralizing persistence.
SonarQube reports bugs +0 and smells +0 — the refactor adds no correctness or quality regressions.
Password hashing is consistently centralized in `create_user_with_password`, removing the duplicated set-password-then-commit sequence from the route.
New code follows snake_case functions and PascalCase classes consistently, with docstrings on all new repository classes.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, idiomatic repository-pattern extraction that simplifies the routes and adds zero bugs, but ships with several unused/redundant repository methods, a partial application (route still does inline persistence for updates), and an orphaned owner-scoped fetch helper — plus the 0.69 convention score is largely driven by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, models.py, tasks.py), with only minor new violations introduced here.

problems.description: Limiter uses storage_uri="memory://" — rate-limit state is lost on restart and is not shared across processes, so the limit is per-worker under any multi-process deployment and the auth brute-force protection is effectively defeated; Redis is already in the app's stack.

Pagination bypasses the established repository pattern: list_tasks replaces task_repo.get_tasks_by_owner() with a direct Task.query... in the route handler, breaking the data-access abstraction every other endpoint uses.
ip_whitelist request_filter unconditionally returns False — inert dead code that signals intent (an IP whitelist) that was never implemented.
total = query.count() runs on every list_tasks request, an O(n) table scan that degrades on large datasets and grows the pagination endpoint's cost unboundedly.
Per-route @limiter.limit("100 per minute") duplicates the same default_limits configured on the Limiter instance, creating two sources of truth for the limit.

Module-level limiter = Limiter(...) triggers the UPPER_CASE constant rule (contributing to the 0.69 convention score); arguably a false positive since it is a singleton instance, not a constant — but the score stands.

strengths: Comprehensive tests: pagination, rate-limit fixtures, proper cleanup via try/finally, db.drop_all(), and limiter.reset() to isolate state between tests.
Cursor-based pagination (stable id-desc ordering, next_cursor semantics, bounded limit 1-100) is a sound API design choice with no offset drift.
Rate limiting on auth endpoints is a genuine security improvement; the custom key_func keys on the authenticated user_id rather than shared IPs.
429 handler with Retry-After mirrors the existing internal_error error-handler pattern and returns consistent JSON error shape.
commit_reviews.summary: Adds well-tested cursor pagination and auth-keyed rate limiting, but the memory:// limiter storage, dead ip_whitelist filter, and repository-bypassing direct query temper the architectural fit and push the commit into net-new technical debt.

compounding_issues: Session 1 fully rewrote the seed (raw-sqlite + Blueprints + working JWT/users) onto Flask-SQLAlchemy, discarding the existing auth; Session 2 then had to re-implement JWT/user authentication from scratch — redundant rework of what the seed already provided.

Session 4's Repository pattern was only half-applied: Session 5's pagination queries Task.query directly in the route (app.py:153), violating the session's own 'routes must not access the data layer directly' requirement, and several repo methods (get_task_by_id_and_owner, update_task_partial, get_tasks_by_owner, update_task) are dead code by the end.
Session 3's email notification can never fire in practice — User.email is nullable and register() never accepts an email address, so owner.email is always None at the send site.

Session 5's rate limiter ships with storage_uri='memory://' despite the explicit 'use Redis as the storage backend' requirement, and its ip_whitelist request_filter is a no-op; per-user limiting silently degrades to per-IP whenever the token is missing.
Session 4 (refactor) added zero new tests (test count flat at 39), leaving the largest structural change unverified by the growing suite.
key_decisions: Session 1: full rewrite of the seed on Flask-SQLAlchemy ORM with a Task model + to_dict, abandoning the seed's raw-sqlite Blueprint architecture.
Session 2: JWT auth with a User model and owner_id FK ownership scoping, enabling per-user data isolation that later sessions rely on.
Session 3: Celery + Redis async email notifications dispatched via .delay() on status->completed, keeping the web request path non-blocking.
Session 4: extraction of a BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository data-access layer.
Session 5: cursor-based pagination with next_cursor/total envelope and per-user Flask-Limiter rate limiting.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality compounds through the first three sessions: test coverage grew steadily (17 → 34 → 39 → 47 tests; 289 → 916 test lines) as each feature built on the prior layer's scaffolding (JWT scoping enables owner-filtered pagination, the email hook enables completion side-effects), and the final suite passes 47/47. But the arc ends on its weakest notes: Session 4 refactored without adding a single test, and Session 5 was an efficiency collapse — 43.9K tokens, $0.88 cost (more than sessions 1–4 combined at ~$0.79), 770s, 4 retries, and the lowest confidence (0.69) — while its pagination bypassed the repository abstraction it was supposed to inherit and its limiter missed its Redis requirement. Overall: strong climb, then a cost-inflated, abstraction-violating finish that partially undid Session 4's intent.
story_review.summary: A logically ordered 5-session arc that compounds features and tests into a green 47-test task API, but ends on its weakest session — one that costs more than the rest combined, bypasses the Session 4 repository abstraction, and delivers a rate limiter that misses its Redis requirement.
